newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Iran scores initial victory in court case vs U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iran scores initial victory in court case vs U.S..

text.p: Iran scored an initial victory in a complex legal battle with the United States on Thursday when the International Court of Justice ruled it could hear a dispute over the destruction of Iranian oil platforms by U.S. warships.

The U.N. court's decision was a setback for Washington which had argued that Iran could not found the case, dealing with events which took place in the late 1980s, on the basis of the 1955 Treaty of Amity between the two countries.
Presiding judge Mohammed Bedjaoui of Algeria said the court had overwhelmingly rejected Washington's objections.

"The court rejects, by 14 votes to two, the preliminary objection of the United States of America according to which the treaty of 1955 does not provide any basis for the jurisdiction of the court," he said.

The 16 judges voted by the same margin that the court had jurisdiction to consider Iran's claims that the destruction of the oil platforms in October 1987 and April 1988 violated international law and that the United States should pay damages.
The disputed events date back to the final stages of the 1980-88 war between Iran and Iraq when the United States sent naval forces to the Gulf to protect international shipping.
Washington had urged the court to throw the case out, arguing that the strikes were a legitimate response to Iranian attacks on a U.S. frigate and an oil tanker sailing under the U.S. flag.
Tehran took the case to The Hague in 1992, arguing that the 1955 Treaty of Amity, Economic Relations and Consular Rights provided a basis for the U.N. court to settle the dispute.
The United States contended that the treaty governed commercial and consular affairs and that political and military matters fell outside its scope.
Thursday's ruling clears the way for further proceedings to consider the issues at the heart of the dispute. This "merits phase" of the case is expected to take several years.
The head of Iran's delegation, Mohammed Zahedin Labaff, said he was "delighted" with the court's decision.
"It is a rightful and just decision and a fair reading of the Treaty of Amity," he said.
U.S. State Department lawyer Michael Matheson said the jurisdiction ruling did not imply that the court agreed with Iran on the rights and wrongs of the underlying dispute.
"The court's decision in no way suggests that it agreed with Iran on the merits of the case...We shall defend this vigorously on the merits and continue to deny U.S. actions were unlawful."
Matheson said the United States was also considering a countersuit against Iran for damage caused to U.S. vessels.
